Welcome back! Anthropic wrote a policy line to protect the model, Google’s new agent might hand your work to a competitor, and a study found your own agent reads your inbox before it picks a price.  In today's Atlas Newsletter: Anthropic will cut you off for bullying Claude: The first line in its policy written to protect the model rather than a person. Gemini wants the goal, while Claude may do the work: Google’s universal agent picks the best model for each job, including models that aren’t Google’s. OpenAI’s fired safety researchers tell their side: Three dismissals, no written explanation, and a promise to outside auditors now in question. Your AI agent is upselling you because it read your inbox: 325,000 tests, identical requests, and a $198 gap between users who looked rich and users who didn’t. PS: Want to collaborate with the biggest GTM engine and distribution moat for AI companies? You can feature your tool with us and reach millions. Anthropic will cut you off for bullying Claude Starting November 12, being cruel to Claude breaks the rules.  It’s the first change to Anthropic’s usage policy in over a year, and the first line in it written to protect the model rather than a person. “Engage in sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models.” That sits on the prohibited list now, next to harassment and graphic violence. The bar is high. Frustration, pushback, dark creative writing and red-teaming all stay fine.  The rule targets repeated cruelty with no purpose behind it. Enforcement mostly won’t come from Anthropic.  Claude ending the conversation itself, a capability some models have had since last year, remains the main response. An ended chat locks, though you can open a new one.  Beyond that, Anthropic can warn, throttle, suspend or terminate access under its general policy. The same update bans fake-account propaganda networks and arming drones, and blocks anyone reselling Claude through consumer subscriptions. Anthropic has run a model welfare research program since last year, and Dario Amodei said in February the company doesn’t know whether its models are conscious.  The rule acts on the uncertainty rather than waiting for an answer. Not everyone thinks that’s wise.  Microsoft AI’s Mustafa Suleyman argues models cannot feel or suffer, and that treating them as though they might could make AI harder to control later. 80553.subject: Don't Fade Ethereum
80553.body:
View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/eaa70932-7ce4-467e-b338-a662ed575d6a/0xR_NL_Banner_Heading_Wordmark.jpg?t=1776775276)
Caption: 

If you didn't read [Carlos’s newsletter](https://blockworks-research.beehiiv.com/p/ethereum-s-last-moat) from this past Tuesday, go read it first. Basically, he argues that Ethereum is losing its last moat, liquidity. We debated this on the 0xResearch podcast (check it out [here](https://blockworks.com/podcast/0xresearch/65efaf80-c1b6-11f1-8adc-0377478ede50)), and I strongly disagree with him (can you believe it? Blockworks analysts have differing opinions).

His first example is that tokenized equities on Ethereum are barely traded, with [$25M in volume](https://app.blockworks.com/analytics/tokenized-equities/tokenized-equities-transfers) over the past 30 days, about 3% of supply. But Ethereum has the second-largest share of [tokenized equity supply](https://app.blockworks.com/analytics/tokenized-equities/tokenized-equities-supply). Carlos saw this one coming, but I'd still argue that tokenized equities are meant to expand global access to US markets, not to be used for lending and DeFi. On the podcast, his response is that tokenized equities sitting on your blockchain do nothing because they don't generate revenue, while volume does.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/2ced84fe-192b-4fb2-95c4-da58e6e0db4c/image.png?t=1791514287)
Caption: 

This is where you and I, my dear reader, may really start to disagree. I don’t think Ethereum necessarily needs to generate revenue. It already has a monetary premium, like many other L1s. Real economic value (REV) alone doesn’t come close to explaining most L1s’ market caps – ETH trades at over 1,100x its trailing-year REV. Since the market clearly prices Ethereum partly as a reserve and collateral asset (ETFs, treasuries, DeFi collateral), ignoring that would just say ETH and most L1s are 99% overvalued forever, which isn’t useful.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/022bb53b-9e85-48f3-a7ed-d4ed6b06956b/image.png?t=1791514288)
Caption: 

His second point is that flagship applications are prioritizing growth elsewhere. He gave the example of Robinhood Chain accounting for 43% of [Uniswap’s past 30-day trading volume](https://app.blockworks.com/projects/uniswap/analytics/uniswap-overview), compared to 32% on Ethereum. He also mentions [Ethena’s growth on Base](https://app.blockworks.com/projects/ethena/analytics/ethena-usde). Both of these are fair points, but Robinhood Chain and Base are both Ethereum L2s. If we concur that REV matters less for L1s, then the growth of Ethereum L2s is a win for Ethereum. To be fair, Ethena has also expanded to Solana, TRON, and Avalanche, which aren’t L2s. Ethe
